newsitem.title: USA: Dollar up on Fed, European Union meetings.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up on Fed, European Union meetings.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 20 - The dollar posted modest gains against major currencies Friday as currency traders squared their books before European finance ministers meet this weekend in Dublin, Ireland, and the Federal Reserve convenes on Tuesday.
The talks in Dublin Castle, which start in earnest on Saturday, are seen as essential for keeping considerable political momentum behind launching a single European currency in January of 1999.

The meeting comes amid an intense scramble by European Union governments led by Germany and France to bring their 1997 budget deficits in line with the Maastricht Treaty criteria for economic and monetary union.

Some currency traders were optimistic that the Dublin talks would yield progress. As a result, the German mark weakened against the dollar and other European currencies because the mark would become less important as a safe haven currency if monetary union came into being.

"As time goes on, it seems like the countries, France and Germany, seem to be determined to try and get their budgetary matters in accord with Maastricht targets," said Tom Benfer, director, foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal.
"So people feel the convergence is going to happen eventually. So that's why the mark was sold off in overnight trading."
The French franc had soared to a two-month high against the mark Friday, but the German currency managed to cut its losses against the franc and other currencies including the dollar in New York.
In late New York trading, the dollar stood at 1.5160 marks late Friday, up from 1.5136 marks late Thursday. The dollar traded at 109.96 Japanese yen, up from 109.44 yen.

Speculation about whether the Fed will hike interest rates on Tuesday to head off any inflationary pressures also has preoccupied the foreign exchange market. Higher rates tend to help the U.S. currency by making dollar-denominated deposits more attractive to foreign investors.

Early in the week, a Reuter report that eight out of 12 district banks in the Federal Reserve System had requested an increase in the discount rate, now at 5 percent, heightened expectations that the central bank might decide to raise rates at Tuesday's meeting of its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
By Friday, currency traders had largely priced into dollar exchange rates the possibility that the Fed may increase rates by one-quarter percentage point, traders said.
In light of this view, there was some reluctance to sell or "short" dollars and a preference to buy or be "long" dollars before Fed policy-makers meet on Tuesday.
"Given the Dublin meeting and given the FOMC meeting on Tuesday, it's difficult to find a reason to be short dollars," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
In other trading, the British pound rose moderately to $1.5557 on Friday from $1.5532 on Thursday. The dollar fell to 1.2390 Swiss francs from 1.2428 francs and to Canadian $1.3670 from C$1.3705.
